554.title: More blessed to give (Acts 20:17–38)
554.hook: Paul's farewell at Miletus; they weep and kneel on the shore
554.howItsDone: Catholics practice almsgiving, one of the three traditional disciplines of Lent alongside prayer and fasting, and give to the poor through parish collections and works of mercy throughout the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eutychus, asleep in the window while Paul talked till dawn. Your line was even Paul went on. Whose long story did you sit through kindly? Day five hundred fifty-four.

A beach at Miletus, on the coast of Asia. Paul is in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, so he doesn't go up to Ephesus, where he spent about three years. Instead he sends for the elders of the Ephesian church to come down to the shore. They walk some thirty miles to meet him. And he gives them the only speech in Acts that Paul makes to Christians, a farewell. He tells them plainly: I don't know what will happen to me in Jerusalem, except that prison and hardship are waiting. And you will not see my face again.
screen: `A BEACH AT MILETUS.` → `THE ELDERS OF EPHESUS.` → `YOU WILL NOT SEE MY FACE AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Paul's farewell sounds like a man setting his affairs in order. He reminds them how he lived among them: serving the Lord with humility and tears, holding nothing back, teaching in public and from house to house. He tells them to keep watch over the flock, like shepherds. Then he holds up his hands. I've coveted no one's silver or gold or clothing. These hands, he says, worked for my own needs and for those who were with me. And then he gives them a saying of Jesus. In the King James: "remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive." Here's the surprise. Those words of Jesus aren't in any of the four Gospels. Matthew, Mark, Luke and John never record them. This is a saying of Jesus preserved only here, in Paul's mouth, passed along by Luke. One sentence of Jesus kept alive by people who remembered it, and almost lost. Notice what Paul does with it. He isn't asking the elders for money. He's showing them his own work-worn hands and saying: this is how to lead. Give. Then the ending, one of the most tender scenes in Acts. Paul kneels down on the shore and prays with them all. They weep, embrace him, and kiss him, grieving most of all, the text says, because he told them they would not see his face again. And they walk him to the ship.
screen: `HUMILITY, TEARS, NOTHING HELD BACK.` · `THESE HANDS WORKED FOR MY NEEDS.` · `A SAYING FOUND IN NO GOSPEL.` · `KNEELING ON THE SHORE.` · then, large: `MORE BLESSED TO GIVE THAN TO RECEIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give something today. Settle, and breathe. Look at your hands, the way Paul held up his. What have they given lately? Now think of one thing you could give today, freely, without being asked. Not necessarily money. Time, a meal, a compliment you meant to say, help with a task, something you own that someone else needs more. Picture handing it over and walking away without waiting for thanks. Notice how that feels. If you pray, you can offer your hands for whatever giving the day brings. The bell holds the time.
More blessed to give. A saying of Jesus found in no Gospel, remembered by Paul on a beach, as he said goodbye. Today's word.
Your line: more blessed to give. Today, give one thing away freely, and don't wait for thanks. Day five hundred fifty-four.

myth: it is more blessed to give than to receive is in one of the Gospels
it isn't in any of the four Gospels. Paul quotes it as Jesus' words in Acts.
Paul asked the elders for money in his farewell
he showed his own hands and said they had worked for his needs.
the elders wept because they would not see him again
that grieved them most of all, the text says.

fork.setup: you're Paul, saying goodbye forever to people you've taught for three years. what do you leave them?
options: a list of rules to follow.
your example, and a saying of Jesus about giving.
instructions to send you money.
fork.reveal: he points to how he lived, holds up his working hands, and quotes Jesus: it is more blessed to give than to receive.

original.note: Greek: blessed, the same word family as the Beatitudes. more blessed is it to give.

trapdoor: what you thought: a proverb from the Gospels.
what it means: a saying of Jesus remembered by Paul at a tearful farewell, as he holds up his own work-worn hands.
what a scholar hears: sayings of Jesus found outside the four Gospels are called agrapha, unwritten sayings. Acts 20:35 is the best known of them in the New Testament.

555.title: Arrested (Acts 21–22)
555.hook: a riot in the Temple and Paul tells his own story
555.howItsDone: In Catholic parishes, adults entering the Church often share their faith story with sponsors and the community during their preparation, and Catholics speak of giving witness by telling plainly what God has done in their lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the farewell on the beach at Miletus. Your line was more blessed to give. What did you give away? Day five hundred fifty-five.

Paul reaches Jerusalem. Friends along the way had begged him not to go. A prophet named Agabus even tied his own hands and feet with Paul's belt to show what was coming. Paul went anyway. In Jerusalem, James and the elders welcome him, and to show he still honors the Law, Paul goes to the Temple to complete a vow of purification with four other men. He's a Jew, worshiping in the Temple of his people. And that's where it all breaks loose.
screen: `AGABUS AND THE BELT.` → `PAUL GOES ANYWAY.` → `TO THE TEMPLE, TO KEEP A VOW.`

segments.voice: Some visitors from Asia see Paul in the Temple and shout that he has brought Greeks into the holy place. He hadn't. They'd seen him in the city earlier with Trophimus, a Gentile from Ephesus, and assumed. Rumors move faster than facts. The crowd seizes Paul, drags him out, and the gates are shut. They're trying to kill him when word reaches the Roman commander of the garrison, who runs down with soldiers. The beating stops. Paul is chained and carried up the steps of the barracks, because the crowd is so violent. And at the top of the steps, bruised, in chains, Paul asks to speak. The commander is surprised he speaks Greek. Paul says, in the King James, "I am a man which am a Jew of Tarsus, a city in Cilicia, a citizen of no mean city." Then he turns and speaks to the crowd in their own language, Hebrew or Aramaic, and they fall quiet. What does he say? Not an argument. His story. I was brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel. I persecuted this Way. On the road to Damascus a light shone around me, and I heard a voice: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" Then a devout man named Ananias came and said, Brother Saul, receive thy sight. That's all. What happened to me. They listen, until he says the Lord sent him to the Gentiles. Then the uproar starts again. Later, about to be flogged, Paul quietly asks the centurion whether it's lawful to scourge a Roman citizen who hasn't been condemned. It isn't. The flogging stops.
screen: `A RUMOR IN THE TEMPLE.` · `CHAINED ON THE BARRACKS STEPS.` · `A JEW OF TARSUS, ASKING TO SPEAK.` · `SAUL, SAUL, WHY PERSECUTEST THOU ME?` · then, large: `HE TELLS WHAT HAPPENED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell your story simply. Settle, and breathe. If someone asked you why you're on this path, practicing, listening, whatever brought you here, what would you say? Not an argument. Just what happened. Who you were before. One moment that changed something. Where you are now. Try it in three short sentences, in your head. It doesn't have to be dramatic. A quiet story told honestly is still yours. If you pray, you can thank God for one moment in it. The bell holds the time.
Arrested. Paul, seized in the Temple over a rumor, rescued by Roman soldiers, and given the steps of a barracks to tell his own story. Today's word.
Your line: tell what happened. Today, if anyone asks why you do what you do, tell them simply and honestly. Day five hundred fifty-five.

pairs: the Ephesian they assumed Paul brought in

myth: Paul really did bring a Gentile into the Temple
he hadn't. people had seen him in the city with Trophimus and assumed.
Paul went to the Temple to keep a vow
James and the elders suggested it, to show he still honored the Law.
Paul answered the crowd with a theological argument
he told his own story: who he was, the road to Damascus, and Ananias.

fork.setup: you're Paul, chained, bruised, carried up the barracks steps away from a furious crowd. what do you do?
options: stay quiet and let the soldiers take you in.
ask to speak to the crowd, and tell them your story.
demand your rights as a Roman at once.
fork.reveal: he asks to speak, the crowd falls silent, and he tells them in their own language what happened to him. he mentions his citizenship only later, when they're about to flog him.

original.note: Greek: in the Hebrew tongue, how Paul addressed the crowd. scholars think it means Aramaic, the everyday language.

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul was arrested for preaching Jesus.
what it means: a false rumor sets off a riot, and Paul, in chains, uses his moment not to argue but to tell what happened to him.
what a scholar hears: this is the second of three tellings of Paul's conversion in Acts. Roman law forbade flogging an uncondemned citizen, which is why the centurion stops cold.

556.title: Almost (Acts 26)
556.hook: King Agrippa says almost thou persuadest me
556.howItsDone: Catholics are encouraged to examine their consciences regularly, often at night, noticing what they have left undone as well as done, and many bring those things to the sacrament of reconciliation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul arrested in the Temple, telling his story from the barracks steps. Your line was tell what happened. Did anyone ask? Day five hundred fifty-six.

Two years pass. Paul sits in custody in Caesarea, on the coast, while governors come and go. Then a new governor, Festus, gets a royal visit: King Agrippa the Second and his sister Bernice arrive with great pomp, the text says, with commanders and the city's leading men. Festus has a prisoner he doesn't know what to do with, and the king is curious. So Paul is brought in, in chains, to a hall full of power. And he tells his story for the third time in Acts.
screen: `TWO YEARS IN CAESAREA.` → `A KING ARRIVES WITH GREAT POMP.` → `A PRISONER IN A HALL OF POWER.`

segments.voice: Paul tells it again: the road, the light at midday brighter than the sun, the voice. This time he includes a line he hasn't mentioned before. The voice said, in the King James, "it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks," like an ox kicking the goad that steers it. Paul had been fighting what was pulling him. He tells how he was sent to open eyes and turn people from darkness to light. Festus can't take it. He shouts: "Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad." Paul answers calmly, I am not mad, most noble Festus. Then he turns to the king. King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do. And Agrippa replies with the line people still quote: "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian." There's that word again from Antioch, Christian, in a king's mouth. What did Agrippa mean? Honestly, nobody's sure. The Greek is two short words, en oligo, in a little. It could mean almost, or in such a short time, or with so little effort. The Douay-Rheims reads it as in a little. He might be moved; he might be brushing Paul off with a smile. Paul's answer is beautiful either way: I would to God that not only you but all who hear me today were both almost, and altogether such as I am, "except these bonds." Picture him raising his chained hands. Then the king rises, and the hearing is over. Agrippa remarks this man could have gone free if he hadn't appealed to Caesar. So to Rome he goes.
screen: `HARD TO KICK AGAINST THE PRICKS.` · `THOU ART BESIDE THYSELF.` · `ALMOST THOU PERSUADEST ME.` · `EXCEPT THESE BONDS.` · then, large: `ALMOST, AND ALTOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't stop at almost. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've almost done for a long time. Almost called. Almost forgiven. Almost started. Almost gone to confession, or to Mass, or to the doctor. Whatever it is, name it quietly. Notice what has kept it at almost: fear, pride, the schedule, a little embarrassment. Now picture the next small step, just one, that would move it from almost to altogether. If you pray, you can offer that one step. The bell holds the time.
Almost. King Agrippa's answer to Paul, maybe moved, maybe joking, and Paul's wish that everyone be not almost but altogether. Today's word.
Your line: almost. Today, take one small, real step on something you've only almost done for too long. Day five hundred fifty-six.

fork.setup: you're Paul. the king has just said, almost thou persuadest me. what do you say?
options: press him hard to decide now.

fork.reveal: he wishes that all who hear him were almost and altogether such as he is, except these bonds. then the king rises and the hearing ends.

original.note: Greek: in a little. Agrippa's two words, which may mean almost, in so short a time, or with so little effort.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king nearly became a Christian.
what it means: Paul tells his story to a king, and the king's reply is so brief and slippery that nobody can say whether he was moved or mocking.
what a scholar hears: en oligō is ambiguous; the KJV says almost, the Douay in a little. this is also the second of only three times the word Christian appears in the New Testament.

557.title: Shipwreck (Acts 27–28:10)
557.hook: a storm, a wreck, everyone saved, and a viper on Malta
557.howItsDone: In Malta, the feast of Saint Paul's Shipwreck on February 10 is a public holiday with Mass and a procession, and Catholics there honor Paul as the island's father in faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Agrippa's slippery answer to Paul. Your line was almost. Did you take one step past almost? Day five hundred fifty-seven.

Acts 27 reads like a sea novel, and it's written in the first person plural: we set sail, we were driven, we were cast ashore. The narrator was on board. Paul is a prisoner bound for Rome under a centurion named Julius. It's late in the sailing season. Paul warns them that this voyage will bring damage and loss. The ship's master and owner want to push on to a better harbor, and the centurion listens to them, not to the prisoner. A gentle south wind blows. They set out. And then a violent northeaster comes down off the island of Crete.
screen: `WE SET SAIL: THE NARRATOR WAS ON BOARD.` → `PAUL WARNS THEM.` → `THE NORTHEASTER HITS.`

segments.voice: The ship can't face the wind, so they let it drive them. They throw cargo overboard, then the ship's tackle. For many days neither sun nor stars appear, and the text says all hope of being saved was taken away. Then Paul stands up among them. Be of good cheer, he says, an angel of God stood by me tonight: not one life will be lost, only the ship. On the fourteenth night, near land, Paul urges everyone to eat, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "for there shall not an hair of the head of any of you perish." Then he takes bread, gives thanks to God in front of them all, breaks it, and begins to eat. And everyone eats. Two hundred seventy-six people, Luke counts. At daylight they run the ship aground and it breaks apart. The soldiers plan to kill the prisoners so none escape, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them. Swimmers swim, the rest float on planks, and, the text says, they all got safe to land. The island is Malta. The islanders show them unusual kindness and light a fire in the rain. Paul gathers a bundle of sticks, and a viper comes out from the heat and fastens on his hand. The islanders say: a murderer, justice won't let him live. Paul shakes it into the fire and nothing happens. They wait for him to swell up. When he doesn't, they change their minds and say he's a god. Luke tells it with a straight face. Malta still keeps the feast of Saint Paul's Shipwreck every February tenth.
screen: `NO SUN, NO STARS, NO HOPE.` · `AN ANGEL STOOD BY ME.` · `BREAD BROKEN IN THE STORM.` · `A VIPER IN THE FIRE.` · then, large: `THEY ALL GOT SAFE TO LAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay calm for others. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place where people around you are anxious: a family worry, a shaky job, a friend in a storm. Paul didn't pretend the storm was small. He just ate, gave thanks, and helped others eat. Picture yourself being the steady one in that room for a minute. Slow breath. A plain kind word. Maybe a meal. Let your own breathing slow down now, and imagine it slowing someone else's. If you pray, you can pray for the people in your boat. The bell holds the time.
Shipwreck. Fourteen days in a storm, bread broken on a sinking ship, everyone saved, and a viper on Malta. Today's word.
Your line: not a hair shall perish. Today, when someone near you is in a storm, be the calm one. Day five hundred fifty-seven.

Acts 27 is told in the first person plural.

fork.setup: you're Paul. fourteen days of storm, no one has eaten, everyone is terrified. what do you do?
options: pray alone in a corner.
urge everyone to eat, give thanks, break bread and eat first.
help the sailors lower the lifeboat.
fork.reveal: he promises not a hair will be lost, takes bread, gives thanks before them all, breaks it and eats. they all take heart and eat.

original.note: Greek: Melita, the island where they came ashore, Malta.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle adventure at sea.
what it means: a prisoner becomes the calm center of a ship in a storm, breaking bread and keeping everyone alive.

what a scholar hears: Acts 27 is one of the 'we' passages, and its sailing details are prized by historians of ancient seafaring. Paul's taking bread, giving thanks and breaking it echoes the Last Supper's words.

558.title: Rome, unhindered (Acts 28:30–31)
558.hook: Paul under house arrest, welcoming all, preaching with confidence
558.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Saints Peter and Paul together on June 29, and pilgrims to Rome visit Paul's tomb at the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, on the road to Ostia.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shipwreck, and every soul brought safe to Malta. Your line was not a hair shall perish. Were you the calm one for someone? Day five hundred fifty-eight.

On day five hundred thirty-four, at the very start of Acts, Jesus told his friends they would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, in Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. Since then we've followed the story out of the upper room, through Samaria and the desert road, to Antioch, across the sea to Philippi, Athens and Corinth, and through a shipwreck. Today it arrives in the capital of the world as Luke's readers knew it. And Paul walks into Rome as a prisoner.
screen: `JERUSALEM, JUDEA, SAMARIA.` → `ANTIOCH, PHILIPPI, ATHENS.` → `AND NOW, ROME.`

segments.voice: As Paul nears the city on the Appian Way, believers from Rome walk out to meet him, at the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. Luke says that when Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage. Even an apostle needed friends to show up. In Rome he's allowed to live by himself, with a soldier guarding him. He calls together the leaders of the Jewish community and speaks with them all day, from morning to evening. Some are persuaded, some are not, and they leave still discussing among themselves. Then come the last two verses of the book. In the King James: "And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him, Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him." That's how Acts ends. Not with Paul's trial. Not with his death. The last word in the Greek is akolutos: unhindered, without hindrance. A man in chains, renting a room, opening his door to whoever comes, and the word is not chained. Why does Luke stop there? Nobody knows for certain. Maybe he wrote before the trial ended. Maybe he wanted the story to stay open, because it isn't finished. Catholic tradition holds that Paul was later martyred in Rome under Nero, beheaded, and buried on the road to Ostia, where the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls now stands. The Church keeps his feast with Peter's on June twenty-ninth.
screen: `FRIENDS WALK OUT TO MEET HIM.` · `A ROOM, A GUARD, AN OPEN DOOR.` · `HE RECEIVED ALL THAT CAME.` · `THE BOOK ENDS OPEN.` · then, large: `WITHOUT HINDRANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome whoever comes. Settle, and breathe. Paul couldn't go anywhere, so he let the world come to him. Picture your own small room today: your desk, your kitchen, your phone. Who might come through it? An unexpected call, a neighbor, a coworker with a question, a kid with a long story. Decide now to receive them, the way Paul received all that came in. Not grudgingly. With the door open. If you pray, you can thank God for the friends who walked out to meet you when you needed it. The bell holds the time.
Rome. Where Acts ends, with Paul in a rented room, welcoming everyone, preaching without hindrance. Today's word.

Your line: without hindrance. Today, open your door to whoever comes. And that's the Acts of the Apostles: witnesses, Pentecost, deacons, the road to Damascus, the council, Lydia, the jail, Athens, the shipwreck, and Rome. Tomorrow, the letters. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

fork.setup: you're Paul, under house arrest in Rome, with a soldier at your side. you can't go out. what do you do?
options: wait quietly for your trial.
open your door and receive everyone who comes.
write to Caesar demanding release.
fork.reveal: for two whole years he receives all who come, preaching with all confidence. Acts ends there, on the word unhindered.

original.note: Greek: unhindered, without hindrance. the very last word of the Acts of the Apostles.

trapdoor: what you thought: Acts ends with Paul's death in Rome.
what it means: it ends with a prisoner in a rented room, welcoming all, preaching freely: the story left open.
what a scholar hears: the last word is akōlytōs, unhindered. Paul's martyrdom under Nero comes from early tradition, such as Clement of Rome and later writers, not from Acts.

559.title: How Paul wrote
559.hook: letters dictated to real churches with real problems, before the gospels were written
559.howItsDone: At Sunday Mass, Catholics usually hear three readings, and the second is most often from the New Testament letters, many of them Paul's; it is read aloud to the whole assembly, as the letters first were.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rome, and Acts ending on the word unhindered. Your line was without hindrance. Who came through your door? Day five hundred fifty-nine.

Imagine finding a box of your grandparents' letters. Not speeches. Letters. Answers to questions you can't see, jokes you don't get, names you don't know, a worry about money, a fight between cousins, and then, in the middle of it all, a paragraph so beautiful you read it twice. That's what we're opening today. A new part of the path: the letters of the New Testament, and first, the letters of Paul.
screen: `A BOX OF OLD LETTERS.` → `QUESTIONS WE CAN'T SEE.` → `A NEW PART: THE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: The word is epistle, from the Greek epistole, simply a letter, something sent. And here's the first surprise: Paul's letters are older than the Gospels. Most scholars date his first letter to the Thessalonians around the year fifty, which makes it very likely the oldest Christian writing that survives. The Gospels were written down later. So when you read Paul, you're reading the earliest Christian voice we have on paper. Second, Paul usually didn't hold the pen. He dictated to a secretary. At the end of Romans, the secretary even slips in his own greeting. In the King James: "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord." Then Paul often took the pen for the last lines, as a signature. To the Galatians he writes, in the King James: "Ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand." Big letters, in his own writing. Third, these were real letters to real people with real problems. Corinth is split into factions. The Galatians are confused. The Thessalonians are grieving their dead. Paul answers them, scolds them, misses them, and greets friends by name. The letters were carried by hand and read aloud to the whole church. Thirteen letters in the New Testament carry Paul's name. Scholars debate whether he wrote every one himself or whether some come from his close followers; the Church receives all of them as scripture. At Sunday Mass, the second reading is usually from these letters. You're hearing someone else's mail, and it was meant to be shared.
screen: `EPISTOLE: A LETTER, SOMETHING SENT.` · `OLDER THAN THE GOSPELS.` · `DICTATED, THEN SIGNED IN BIG LETTERS.` · `REAL CHURCHES, REAL PROBLEMS.` · then, large: `READ ALOUD TO EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write a short letter to someone. Settle, and breathe. Think of a person you haven't really written to in a long time. Not a text. A letter, even a short one. What would you say to them, if it were the kind of thing that might be kept? Thanks for something specific. A memory. Encouragement for something hard they're facing. Compose three sentences in your head now. Maybe later, write them down, and sign them in your own big letters. If you pray, you can pray for that person as Paul so often did in his opening lines. The bell holds the time.
Epistle. A letter, something sent: Paul's dictated, hand-signed letters to real churches, older than the Gospels, read aloud to everyone. Today's word.
Your line: real letters to real people. Today, write a few honest lines to someone, by hand if you can. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

fork.setup: you're Paul. a church you started, far away, is fighting and confused, and you can't travel there. what do you do?
options: wait until you can visit.
dictate a letter, sign it, and send it with a friend.
let them sort it out themselves.
fork.reveal: that's how most of his letters came to be: real answers to real problems, carried by hand and read aloud.

original.note: Greek: a letter, something sent. from a verb meaning to send to.

trapdoor: what you thought: an epistle is a kind of sermon.
what it means: it's a letter: dictated, signed, carried by hand, and answering real problems in real churches.

what a scholar hears: Paul's letters are the oldest Christian writings we have, from around AD 50 to the 60s. seven are accepted by nearly all scholars as his own; the authorship of the other six is debated.

560.title: Not ashamed (Romans 1:16)
560.hook: the gospel is the power of God unto salvation
560.howItsDone: Many Catholics make the sign of the cross and say grace before meals, including in public, and at Mass they trace a small cross on the forehead, lips and heart before the Gospel is read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how Paul wrote: dictated letters, signed in big handwriting. Your line was real letters to real people. Did you write a few lines to someone? Day five hundred sixty.

Most of us know the small hesitation. You're at a restaurant with coworkers and you wonder whether to make the sign of the cross before you eat. Someone asks what you did on Sunday and you say, oh, not much. Nobody is persecuting you. It's just easier not to mention it. Paul knew that feeling well, and in the letter that opens the New Testament's collection of letters, he answers it in the first chapter.
screen: `THE SIGN OF THE CROSS AT LUNCH?` → `OH, NOT MUCH.` → `PAUL KNEW THAT FEELING.`

segments.voice: Romans is a letter to a church Paul had not founded and had never visited. He's writing ahead, probably from Corinth, introducing himself and his message before he arrives. And though Romans comes first among the letters in your Bible, it isn't the oldest. Paul's letters are arranged roughly by length, longest first. Romans is simply the longest. Near the start, Paul says what the whole letter is about. In the King James: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek." Why would he even mention shame? Because in his world, his message was embarrassing. Crucifixion was the most shameful death Rome had, reserved for slaves and rebels. To say that God's anointed one died on a cross sounded, to many people, ridiculous. And Rome was the capital of honor and power. Paul is about to write to the people at the center of that world, and he begins: I'm not ashamed of this. Notice what he calls the gospel: not an idea or an argument, but power, the Greek word dunamis, the root of our word dynamite. And notice who it's for: everyone who believes, Jew first and also Greek, no one shut out. Catholics have long used a small gesture for this very thing. Before the Gospel at Mass, they trace a small cross on the forehead, lips and heart, as if to say: in my mind, on my lips, in my heart, unashamed.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say grace in public, if you pray. Settle, and breathe. Think of your next meal with other people around, at work, in a restaurant, in a school cafeteria. Picture yourself pausing before you eat. Maybe a sign of the cross. Maybe a few silent words. Maybe just a moment of thanks, eyes open. Notice what you feel imagining it: a flush of self-consciousness, maybe. That's normal. Paul felt the pull too. If grace isn't your practice, picture simply being honest about something you care about, when it would be easier to say not much. The bell holds the time.
Not ashamed. Paul's opening claim to Rome: the gospel of a crucified Messiah is the power of God for everyone who believes. Today's word.

Your line: not ashamed. Today, at one meal, pause and give thanks where others can see. And that's week eighty: more blessed to give, arrested, almost, shipwreck, Rome, epistle, and not ashamed. Day five hundred sixty.

original.note: Greek: to be ashamed of. Paul says, ou gar epaischynomai, for I am not ashamed.

trapdoor: what you thought: not ashamed means being bold about religion.
what it means: in a world where crucifixion meant total disgrace, Paul says the message of a crucified Messiah is God's own power.
what a scholar hears: Romans 1:16–17 is often read as the theme of the whole letter. the word for power, dunamis, gave us dynamite, a name Alfred Nobel took from the Greek.
